entries.topicDescription: Understanding how Android creates, pauses, and destroys activities.

questions.questionText: Which lifecycle callback is called when an Activity is no longer visible to the user?
questions.explanation: onStop() is invoked after onPause() when the Activity is fully hidden.

questions.questionText: Which callback should be used to store transient UI state before an Activity may be recreated?
questions.explanation: Use onSaveInstanceState() to persist small UI state values across process death and configuration changes.

entries.topicDescription: Continuous integration and delivery pipelines for Android apps, including Azure Pipelines.

questions.questionText: In Android CI, which Gradle task is commonly used to run JVM unit tests for the debug variant?
questions.explanation: testDebugUnitTest executes local JVM unit tests for the debug build variant.

questions.questionText: What is a major benefit of dependency and build caching in Android CI/CD pipelines?
questions.explanation: Caching avoids re-downloading dependencies and re-running unchanged work, which reduces pipeline time.

answers.answerText: Faster build times by reusing unchanged artifacts
Automatic app store publishing without credentials
No need to run tests in pull requests

entries.topicDescription: Layered architecture patterns for Android: domain, data, and presentation boundaries.

questions.questionText: In Clean Architecture, where should core business rules and use cases live?
questions.explanation: Business logic belongs in the domain layer so it stays independent of frameworks, UI, and data sources.

questions.questionText: What dependency rule does Clean Architecture enforce?
questions.explanation: Dependencies point inward: outer layers depend on abstractions in inner layers, not the other way around.

answers.answerText: All layers should depend directly on framework classes
Data layer must import UI composables
Outer layers can depend on inner layers, but inner layers must not depend on outer layers
Domain layer should call Android Context APIs directly

entries.topicDescription: Managing object creation and dependencies with Hilt, Koin, and manual DI patterns.

questions.questionText: In Hilt, what annotation is used on a constructor to request dependency injection?
questions.explanation: Applying @Inject to a constructor lets Hilt create that class when its dependencies are available.

questions.questionText: Which annotation provides a single dependency instance for the whole application in Hilt?
questions.explanation: @Singleton scopes a dependency to the application's lifetime when installed in the singleton component.

entries.topicDescription: Runtime application self-protection and obfuscation strategies.

questions.questionText: What is the main goal of code obfuscation tools like DexGuard?
questions.explanation: Obfuscation makes app code harder to reverse engineer by renaming and transforming symbols and logic.

answers.answerText: Make reverse engineering and tampering harder

questions.questionText: What does RASP primarily help detect at runtime?
questions.explanation: RASP checks runtime conditions such as hooking, tampering, or rooted devices and can react defensively.

answers.answerText: Threats like hooking, tampering, and rooted environments
Only Play Store signing key expiry

entries.topicDescription: Fragment lifecycle, communication, and management within Activities and Navigation.

questions.questionText: Which Fragment callback is responsible for inflating and returning the Fragment's UI?
questions.explanation: onCreateView() should inflate and return the Fragment view hierarchy.

questions.questionText: What is a recommended way for two fragments in the same Activity to share UI state?
questions.explanation: An Activity-scoped shared ViewModel is lifecycle-aware and avoids tight coupling between fragments.

answers.answerText: Cast one Fragment to the other and call methods directly
Store shared state in static global variables
Pass data only through manifest placeholders

entries.topicDescription: Core Android building blocks: intents, broadcast receivers, the manifest, and services.

questions.questionText: Which lifecycle method is called when an Activity first becomes visible?
questions.explanation: onStart() is called when the Activity becomes visible to the user, after onCreate() and before onResume().

questions.questionText: What happens to an Activity when the user rotates the device?
questions.explanation: By default, Android destroys and recreates the Activity on configuration changes like rotation. Use ViewModel to survive this.

answers.answerText: The app is restarted from the launcher

entries.topicDescription: Build variants, product flavors, and custom Gradle tasks for Android projects.

questions.questionText: What do product flavors enable in an Android Gradle project?
questions.explanation: Product flavors let you build multiple app variants (for example free vs paid) from one codebase.

answers.answerText: Creating multiple app variants from the same codebase
Automatically replacing all dependencies at runtime
Disabling ProGuard and R8 in release
Removing the need for build types

questions.questionText: Where are Android build types like debug and release typically configured?
questions.explanation: Build types are defined inside the android { buildTypes { ... } } block in the module Gradle build file.

answers.answerText: In the module's build.gradle.kts under android.buildTypes

questions.questionText: In Compose Navigation, what component hosts the navigation graph?
questions.explanation: NavHost is the composable that displays the current destination and manages the navigation back stack.

questions.questionText: How do you pass arguments between destinations in Compose Navigation?
questions.explanation: You define arguments in the route pattern (e.g., 'detail/{id}') and read them from NavBackStackEntry's arguments bundle.

answers.answerText: Define in route pattern and read from NavBackStackEntry arguments

entries.topicDescription: Networking layer patterns for production Android apps.

questions.questionText: Which Ktor client plugin is commonly used to serialize and deserialize JSON payloads?
questions.explanation: ContentNegotiation with a JSON serializer handles request/response body conversion in Ktor Client.

questions.questionText: How can you add an Authorization header to every Ktor client request?
questions.explanation: Install DefaultRequest and set the header there so it is applied to outgoing requests by default.

answers.answerText: Install DefaultRequest and add the Authorization header in its configuration
Put the token in AndroidManifest meta-data
Use NavController arguments for all HTTP headers

entries.topicDescription: Architecture component for managing UI-related data across configuration changes.

questions.questionText: What is the main reason to use a ViewModel in Android?
questions.explanation: ViewModel survives configuration changes and keeps UI state separate from Activity/Fragment lifecycle.

answers.answerText: To retain UI-related data across configuration changes
To replace Room for local persistence
To render composables faster by default
To remove the need for lifecycle-aware components

questions.questionText: Which coroutine scope should be used inside a ViewModel for async work?
questions.explanation: viewModelScope is lifecycle-aware for ViewModel and is cancelled automatically when ViewModel is cleared.

questions.questionText: What is a recommended way to expose mutable state from a ViewModel?
questions.explanation: Keep mutable state private and expose immutable state (StateFlow/LiveData) to prevent external mutation.

answers.answerText: Expose StateFlow publicly and keep MutableStateFlow private
Expose MutableStateFlow directly so UI can update it
Store UI state in Fragment fields only
Use static singleton variables for all screen state

entries.topicDescription: Scheduling deferrable, guaranteed background work with WorkManager.

questions.questionText: When should you prefer WorkManager over a Foreground Service?
questions.explanation: WorkManager is best for deferrable, guaranteed background work that should run even after app restarts. Foreground Service is for user-visible ongoing tasks.

answers.answerText: For guaranteed deferrable background work that can run later
For drawing UI when app is in background
For replacing all coroutines in ViewModel

questions.questionText: What does enqueueUniqueWork() help prevent?
questions.explanation: Unique work ensures only one chain with the same unique name exists according to the chosen ExistingWorkPolicy.

answers.answerText: Creating duplicate background work chains for the same task

questions.questionText: If a Worker returns Result.retry(), what happens next?
questions.explanation: WorkManager reschedules the work using its backoff policy (linear or exponential), then attempts it again later.

answers.answerText: The work is rescheduled and retried later using backoff policy
The work is marked as permanently failed immediately
The worker runs again instantly in a tight loop
All pending work in the app is cancelled

entries.topicDescription: Posting, channeling, and permissioning notifications on modern Android.

questions.questionText: On Android 8.0 (API 26) and above, what must every notification be posted to?
questions.explanation: Since API 26 each notification belongs to a NotificationChannel; a notification with no valid channel isn't shown. Channels let users control each category of notification separately.

questions.questionText: Which runtime permission must an app targeting Android 13 request before it can post notifications?
questions.explanation: POST_NOTIFICATIONS became a runtime permission in Android 13 (API 33). Without it, the app's notifications are not shown.

questions.questionText: After a NotificationChannel has been created, which of its settings can your app still change in code?
questions.explanation: Once a channel exists the user owns its importance, sound and vibration. The app can still update the channel's name and description; to change behavior it must use a new channel ID.

answers.answerText: Its importance, by calling createNotificationChannel again with a new value
Everything, as long as the app targets the latest API level
Nothing at all, including the name

entries.topicDescription: Persisting preferences and files safely: DataStore, app-specific storage, scoped storage, and backups.

questions.questionText: What is a key advantage of DataStore over SharedPreferences?
questions.explanation: DataStore exposes data as a Flow and performs reads and writes asynchronously and transactionally, so it can't block the main thread. It does not encrypt data.

answers.answerText: It allows synchronous reads on the main thread
It is asynchronous and updates data transactionally
It shares data between different apps

questions.questionText: Where should you put a file that you can rebuild and that the system may delete when storage runs low?
questions.explanation: cacheDir is meant for rebuildable data; the system can clear it under storage pressure. filesDir holds durable private data, and getExternalFilesDir is app-specific space on shared storage.

questions.questionText: What happens if two DataStore instances are active for the same file in one process?
questions.explanation: DataStore requires a single instance per file per process; creating a second one for the same file throws an IllegalStateException when both are active. Declare the delegate once at top level or provide a singleton.

answers.answerText: The second instance is silently ignored
The two instances merge their data

entries.topicDescription: Calling HTTP APIs with Retrofit and OkHttp: interfaces, converters, interceptors, authentication, caching and testing.

questions.questionText: What must the base URL passed to Retrofit.Builder end with?
questions.explanation: Retrofit resolves the relative paths on your annotations against the base URL, and it requires the base URL to end with a slash; otherwise building the Retrofit instance throws an IllegalArgumentException.

questions.questionText: With Retrofit suspend functions, what does an HttpException mean?
questions.explanation: HttpException means the server responded with a non-2xx status code. A failure to get any response, such as no connection or a timeout, surfaces as an IOException.

answers.answerText: The device has no network connection
The JSON could not be parsed
The server replied with a non-2xx status code

questions.questionText: Which OkHttp interface is called when a server answers 401 so you can supply new credentials and retry the request?
questions.explanation: An Authenticator is invoked on an authentication challenge such as 401. It can return a new request with fresh credentials, or null to give up.

entries.topicDescription: Layered architecture patterns for Android: domain, data, and presentation boundaries.

questions.questionText: In unidirectional data flow, what travels from the ViewModel down to the UI?
questions.explanation: State flows down from the ViewModel to the UI, and events flow up from the UI to the ViewModel. The UI never changes state directly.

questions.questionText: In MVI, which component computes the new state from the current state and a user intent?
questions.explanation: A reducer is a pure function that takes the current state and an intent and returns the next state, which makes every state transition explicit and easy to test.

questions.questionText: Why should a ViewModel not hold a NavController?
questions.explanation: A NavController belongs to the UI. A ViewModel outlives the UI, so holding one leaks it and couples the ViewModel to the framework. Expose what should happen and let the composable navigate.

answers.answerText: Because ViewModels cannot call any function of the Navigation library
Because NavController can only be created in the data layer
Because the ViewModel outlives the UI, so it would leak the NavController and depend on UI framework types

entries.topicDescription: Architecture component for managing UI-related data across configuration changes.

questions.questionText: Which owner should scope a ViewModel that must be shared by all screens of a multi-step flow in Compose Navigation?
questions.explanation: Scoping to the parent navigation graph's back stack entry shares one instance across the flow and clears it when the user leaves the flow, instead of keeping it for the whole Activity.

answers.answerText: Each screen's own back stack entry
The parent navigation graph's back stack entry

questions.questionText: Why is stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) commonly used for UI state?
questions.explanation: WhileSubscribed(5_000) keeps the upstream running through short gaps such as a configuration change and stops it five seconds after the last collector leaves, so work isn't done while nothing is observing.

answers.answerText: It makes the state survive process death
It runs the upstream on a background thread only
It prevents the StateFlow from ever emitting duplicates
It stops the upstream 5 seconds after the last collector leaves, surviving configuration changes without wasted work

entries.topicDescription: Layered architecture patterns for Android: domain, data, and presentation boundaries.

questions.questionText: In Clean Architecture, where should a repository interface live and where should its implementation live?
questions.explanation: The domain layer declares the interface and the data layer implements it, so the dependency points inward. DI binds the implementation to the interface.

answers.answerText: Interface in the data layer, implementation in the UI layer
Interface in the UI layer, implementation in the domain layer
Interface in the domain layer, implementation in the data layer

entries.topicDescription: Designing a robust networking layer: authentication, TLS, retries, error handling, serialization and headers, independent of the HTTP library.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between HTTP 401 and 403?
questions.explanation: 401 means the request lacks valid credentials (try refreshing the token or signing in). 403 means the user is authenticated but not allowed to do this, so refreshing a token won't help.

answers.answerText: 401 means the server is down and 403 means the resource moved
They are two names for the same error
401 means not allowed, 403 means credentials missing
401: credentials missing or invalid; 403: authenticated but not permitted

questions.questionText: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
questions.explanation: Without jitter, many clients that failed at the same moment retry at the same moments and overload the server again. Randomizing the delay spreads the retries out.

answers.answerText: To stop many clients from retrying at exactly the same time

questions.questionText: Which response header tells a client how long to wait before retrying after a 429 Too Many Requests?
questions.explanation: Retry-After holds either a number of seconds or an HTTP date. When it is present, use it instead of your own backoff delay.

questions.questionText: What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add compared with normal TLS?
questions.explanation: In normal TLS only the server presents a certificate. With mTLS the server also requires a client certificate during the handshake and rejects clients that don't present a trusted one.

answers.answerText: It encrypts the request body a second time
It removes the need for certificate authorities
It makes the connection use HTTP instead of HTTPS
The client also authenticates itself with a certificate
